title: When will smart phones be aid?
html:
As the humanitarian community promotes the importance of information to the affected populations (eg CDAC Network and Internews) and the power of mobile phones in this area, I am left wondering when smart phones will become part of the standard aid package? We already distribute Non-Food Items (NFI) kits - why not include a smart phone with a SIM card.

Given that you can already buy $50 dollar Android phones in Kenya, we have to assume that prices will continue to drop. But why smart phones and not just feature phones? Because we can pre-load them with relevant apps to collect input thus not relying on someone installing “our app”, provide a better service to the affected community (report needs, warn about security concerns, etc), and enable illiterate people to participate (think image based icons and/or video on smart phones versus text-based feature phones).

As well, by giving out phones, we would create an incentive for people to register and keep us updated (especially if we were making cash transfers through them). Imagine the instance where everyone in a refugee camp receives a phone upon arrival. They could receive updates from the humanitarian community, stay connected with their family, browse or listen to online news, and install powerful apps relevant to them (eg health monitoring, client satisfaction tools, etc). The refugees could interact with a wide variety of specialists from outside the camp through their phones which they cannot do now - medical professionals, online education, phyco-social support, and so on. Some might logically ask: will such a change affect the role of the in-country responder. Of course. You would be enabling the affected community to help itself. And, the world to help the refugees. The services provided locally may shift. It would be moving us more towards a Humanitarianism-as-a-Software concept.

The idea might be a bit early for some, but ITU noted, in their 2012 Smart Regulation in Broadband World Summary, that “mobile broadband has grown even faster in terms of the number of actual users and reached an estimated 1.19 billion subscriptions in more than 160 countries by the end of 2011. In developing countries, mobile broadband penetration had reached an estimated 8.5 percent by end 2011, up from 5.3 percent just one year earlier.” They also continued to outline how 130 governments had already or were planning to adopt a national policy, strategy or plan to promote broadband infrastructure (thus extending connectivity to provide universal access to all). 

In The Mobile Wave: How Mobile Intelligence Will Change Everything, Michael Salor discusses the cost of providing connectivity infrastructure to Zinder which is in remote southern Niger. He outlines that “the cost of laying copper in a city of 200,000 like Zinder would be more than $50 million in wiring alone, and at least another $50 million in labor and equipment charges to bury it in trenches. (stringing wire on poles would be in-feasible due to theft of the copper.) Yet, the cell tower infrastructure can be deployed for tens of thousands of dollars, making it a thousand times less expensive.”  At what point can we assume that mobile infrastructure will be cheap and critical enough that it will cover the world. Connectivity, in some ways, could become development aid in partnership with private companies. How long before we consider Connectivity-As-Aid and ensure that everyone is connected?

If electricity was the universal power platform of the industrial revolution then will mobile infrastructure be the driver of the information revolution?

Times are changing and mobile will be a huge enabling factor. Are you ready?

Andrej
teaser: A case for including a smartphone and SIM card in standard aid packages and what refugees could do with them.
seo_description: Why smart phones may belong in aid kits, how connectivity could help affected communities and what it could change.
